title: The impact of base model end of support

opening.headline: When the base model you tuned for ends support, the tuned model will also disappear. At this time, we find out what disappears and what remains.
body: Tuned models are built on top of a specific base model. Therefore, it can only be used for inference while the base model is provided, and when the base model is lowered, the tuning model above it cannot be used as well. The time and money spent on tuning will not translate into a new model.

In this class, we first check the life cycle of a tuning model, distinguish between retuning costs and conversion costs, and look at how to manage training data and evaluation sets, which are assets that remain even when the model changes. Next, the instructor explains a case where a new model replaces the existing tuning.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Describe the impact of end of base model support on tuning models
Distinguish between retuning costs and conversion costs

screens.title: When the basic model goes down, tuning also disappears.
screens.lead: Toggle between the two states to see how the tuning model changes while the base model is provided and after it is toned down.

states.label: While the base model is available
states.body: Tuned models are built on top of a specific base model. As long as the base model is provided, the tuned model can be used for inference as is. If you use the model ID in your calling code, you will receive a response in the same way as the base model. During this period, the tuning effect is maintained, so it is difficult to notice any problems.

states.label: After the basic model goes down
states.body: If the base model is lowered, the tuning model created above it will no longer be usable. The time and money spent on tuning will not carry over to the new model, so processing must be redone on a new base model to achieve the same effect. If you are not aware of when this change occurs, your service may suddenly stop.

screens.outro: First, let us recall the situation of the model we are currently using.

screens.title: To remind you: the end of support schedule for your model
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Do you know the end-of-support schedule for your model?
items.answer: There is a set end date for each model, and that date is written in the provider documentation. If you don't know the schedule, it's difficult to find time to respond. It is safe to have procedures for regular checking.

items.prompt: Is there a tuning model made on top of that model?
items.answer: The tuning model is tied to the schedule of the base model. Keep a list of which tuning models are on top of which base models so you know the scope of impact when schedules come up.

items.prompt: Where is the data used for tuning stored?
items.answer: Training data and evaluation sets are assets that remain even if the model changes. If the storage location is unclear, the data must be recreated from scratch when retuning.

screens.outro: Let's see step by step what life cycle the tuning model follows.

screens.title: Tuning model life cycle flow
screens.lead: Click the Next button to follow the flow step by step as the tuning model is created, used, and then down to the basic model.

visual.alt: A time flow diagram showing that a tuning model is created on top of the base model, goes down as the base model goes down, and data leads to retuning the new model.
labels: End of support for base model

steps.title: 1 left for inference
steps.body: The tuned model remains for inference purposes while the base model is provided. According to OpenAI's documentation, the fine-tuned model can be used for inference until the base model is brought down.

steps.title: 2 go down together
steps.body: When the base model goes down, the tuning model above it goes down as well. The document lists end dates for each model. For example, `gpt-4.1-nano-2025-04-14` and its tuning models will end on October 23, 2026, and `gpt-4.1-2025-04-14` and `gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14` and their tuning models will end on January 14, 2027.

steps.title: 3 Possible range of new tuning
steps.body: The scope of new tuning varies depending on the model and provider. OpenAI's fine-tuning platform is not accessible to new users, and only eligible existing customers can create training jobs until January 6, 2027. However, if the basic model is terminated before then, training for that model also ends.

steps.title: 4 Circumstances on the Gemini side
steps.body: Models that support tweaking are no longer available in the Gemini API and AI Studio; tweaking is supported in the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Even with the same Gemini, the way it can be used varies depending on which product it is tuned with.

steps.title: 5 Continue tuning
steps.body: There is also a method of continuing tuning from an existing tuning model. OpenAI can specify the ID of a previously tuned model as the base model, while Gemini uses an existing tuning model or checkpoint as a starting point with continuous tuning. However, this is only while the base model is alive, and when the base model goes down, this path is also blocked.

screens.outro: Now that we know the life cycle, let’s break down the costs of response into two parts.

screens.title: Retuning costs and conversion costs, data capitalization and portability
screens.lead: Select each tab to see what kind of costs it will cost when the base model goes down, and what assets you will need to leave behind.

tabs.label: retuning cost
tabs.body: This is the cost of retraining on a new base model with the same data. If you already have the data, there is no cost to create the data, but there is a cost for training and evaluation after learning. Hyperparameters may need to be readjusted if the underlying model changes.

tabs.label: conversion cost
tabs.body: This is the cost of moving to a new model. This involves re-running assessments in the new model, re-adjusting prompts, and changing deployment paths. Even if you just move to a new model with prompts without retuning, this conversion cost will be incurred. It must be calculated separately from the retuning cost to avoid omission.

tabs.label: Data capitalization
tabs.body: Training data and evaluation sets are assets that remain even if the model changes. If you keep it separate from the model and store it in a reusable form, you can immediately re-measure and re-tune it on a new model. Tuned weights are tied to a specific model, but the data is not. Cleaning and improving data quality is therefore an investment that will remain valuable regardless of model replacement.

tabs.label: portability
tabs.body: The format of tuning data varies by provider. OpenAI uses the `messages` array format, and Gemini uses its own JSONL format. Therefore, storing the original data in a provider-neutral form and converting it to each format when necessary increases portability.

screens.outro: Now, let's take an example of the judgment made when a new model was released.

screens.title: Case Commentary: When a new model replaces an existing tuning
screens.lead: The instructor explains a hypothetical case. Click the Next button to follow the judgment process.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: A successor model to the basic model that was tuned has been released. It is said that the new model is close to the performance of the previous tuning model with just the prompt. The end schedule for the existing model has also been confirmed.

steps.title: 1 Measured using the same evaluation set
steps.body: Using the archived evaluation set, we apply the improved prompts to the new model and measure it. The baseline is the evaluation value of the existing tuning model. Because there is an evaluation set, you can compare numbers rather than feelings.

steps.title: 2 Look at the gap and choose
steps.body: If the gap is small, switch to the new model without retuning. If a gap remains, re-tuning is performed on the new model using the saved training data. In both cases, data and evaluation sets are the starting point for judgment.

steps.title: 3 Conversion costs added up
steps.body: Add up transition costs such as readjusting prompts and assessments, and changing distribution routes. If you choose to retune, learning costs are also added. It also reflects the difference in call price between the new model and the existing tuning model.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: Tuning models can be replaced, but training data and evaluation sets are still used. By protecting these two assets, we were able to make sound judgments in a short period of time when a new model was released. Without the data and evaluation set, we would have had to start over from scratch to evaluate the performance of the new model.

screens.outro: I will organize the preparation items to prepare for the end of the day.

screens.title: Case Commentary: What to Prepare for a Shutdown
screens.lead: As you select each item, your instructor will explain why you need to prepare for it. Unfold them one by one.

items.prompt: How do we store training data and evaluation sets?
items.answer: Store it separately in its original format. Archiving only in a specific provider's format increases the conversion effort when switching providers. By keeping the versions attached, you can keep track of which model was trained with which data.

items.prompt: How do I manage the list of tuning models?
items.answer: It maintains a list of which base model each tuning model is on and where it is called. Once the baseline model's retirement schedule is confirmed, you'll know immediately which services will be affected.

items.prompt: How do I check the closing schedule?
items.answer: Have a procedure in place to regularly check your model's retirement schedule. If you set an inspection cycle with the person in charge, you will be less likely to miss the schedule.

items.prompt: How do we maintain evaluation standards?
items.answer: Keeping your evaluation criteria independent of the model allows you to re-measure as soon as new models become available. Evaluation sets and scorers should not be tied to a specific model.

items.prompt: What are the chances of achieving your goal without tuning?
items.answer: We always evaluate the likelihood that a new model will be close to the goal based on prompts alone. Then, you can compare the same numbers to determine whether to continue tuning or move to the prompt.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Key theorems and connections
screens.lead: Summary of the impact of end of base model support. As you read, recall the list of tuning models in our service.

paragraphs: Tuned models are tied to the base model. It can only be used while the basic model is available, and when the basic model goes down, it goes down as well. At this time, the tuned weights are not transferred to the new model. Since the support end schedule varies for each model, we manage it in a list.

The response cost is calculated by dividing it into the retuning cost and the switching cost. Retuning is the cost of retraining on a new base model, while transition is the cost of moving evaluation, prompting, and deployment paths.

On the other hand, training data and evaluation sets are assets that remain even if the model changes. Keeping it in its original format allows you to make quick decisions when switching providers or switching to a new model.

Going back to the first question, when the base model goes down, what disappears are the tuned weights, and what remains is the data and evaluation set and the ability to make decisions based on them.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Tuning is tied to the model and data is the asset. This one sentence will help you remember the direction of your preparation. Start by managing your model list, shutdown schedule, and data storage location in one table.

checks.intro: Think about what remains after support ends. Just choose the one that suits you best.
checks.q: If the tuned base model is lowered, the tuned model will no longer be available. What assets can you continue to leverage by moving to the new model?
options: Inference endpoints for existing base models
checks.explain: Tuned weights are tied to a specific base model, but training data and evaluation sets remain even when models change. If you keep it in its original format, you can convert it and use it even when you change providers.

wrong.0: Weights are tied to that base model and are not transferred to the new model.
wrong.2: When the basic model goes down, endpoints cannot be used together.
wrong.3: The money has already been spent and will not carry over to the new model.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Even if the model changes, the data and evaluation set are assets that remain.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Distinguish between what is tied to the model and what is not. Weights, endpoints, and costs are all tied to the model.

checks.intro: Think about the judgment flow when a new model comes out. Just arrange the items in the appropriate order.
checks.q: Put them in order to determine if the new model can replace the existing tune.
items: Measure new models and improvement prompts using the same evaluation set
Look at the gap and decide whether to convert or retune with the saved data.
Add up transition costs, such as readjusting prompts and assessments.
checks.explain: First, measure with the same evaluation set, select conversion or retuning depending on the gap, and then add up the conversion cost to make the decision.
checks.correctFeedback: The order of judgment was arranged correctly.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is out of order. Reframe your judgment by measuring it and ending with adding up the costs.

glossary.def: This means that the provider will no longer offer a specific model version.
This involves retraining on a new base model.
This involves storing learning and evaluation data separately from the model so that they can be reused.
It is to the extent that it can be transferred to another model or provider.

misconceptions.myth: Tuned models can be used permanently.
misconceptions.fact: It is only available while the base model is available. When the base model goes down, it goes down with it.

misconceptions.myth: All you have to do is re-tune and the cost is over.
misconceptions.fact: There are separate transition costs such as evaluation, adjusting prompts, and changing deployment paths.

misconceptions.myth: Learning data can be deleted once learning is complete.
misconceptions.fact: We keep it because it is a key asset for retuning and evaluation. Keeping it in its original format is advantageous when changing providers.

closing.lead: The key points of this class are summarized as follows.
points: Tuning is tied to the model and data is the asset.
When the basic model goes down, the tuning model goes down as well.
Retuning costs and conversion costs are calculated separately.
Keeping the original data and evaluation sets makes comparison easier.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for you to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Are our training data and evaluation sets stored in a form that can be immediately reused even if the model changes?
